entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12866"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> Habakkuk, from a Hebrew root meaning to "embrace," denoting a "favorite" (namely, of God) and a "struggler" (for his country's good). Some ancient authors represent him as belonging to the tribe of Levi; others [Pseudo Epiphanius], to that of Simeon. The inscription to Bel and the dragon in the Septuagint asserts the former; and <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Ha 3:19</reference> perhaps favors this. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 7.29] states that in his time Habakkuk's tomb was shown at Celia in Palestine.<div eID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23985" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> The time seems to have been about 610 B.C. For the Chaldeans attacked Jerusalem in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim, 605 B.C. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">36:9</reference>). And Habakkuk (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Ha 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">6</reference>, &c.) speaks of the Chaldeans as about to invade Judah, but not as having actually done so. In the second chapter he proceeds to comfort his people by foretelling the humiliation of their conquerors, and that the vision will soon have its fulfilment. In the third chapter the prophet in a sublime ode celebrates the deliverances wrought by Jehovah for His people in times past, as the ground of assurance, notwithstanding all their existing calamities, that He will deliver them again. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Ha 3:16</reference> shows that the invader is still coming, and not yet arrived; so that the whole refers to the invasion in Jehoiakim's times, not those under Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. The Apocryphal appendix to Daniel states that he lived to see the Babylonian exile (588 B.C.), which accords with his prophesying early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 610 B.C.<div eID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> The position of the book immediately after Nahum is appropriate; as Nahum treated of the judgments of the Lord on Assyria, for its violence against Israel, so Habakkuk, those inflicted by, and on, the Chaldeans for the same reason.<div eID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> The style is poetical and sublime. The parallelisms are generally regular. Borrowed ideas occur (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Ha 3:19</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> The ancient catalogues imply that his book is part of the canon of Scripture. In the New Testament, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference> quotes <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Ha 2:4</reference> (though not naming him); compare also <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">Ga 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>. <reference osisRef="Acts.13.40">Ac 13:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">41</reference> quotes <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Ha 1:5</reference>. One or two Hebrew words peculiar to Habakkuk occur (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">Ha 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2:6, 16</reference>).<div eID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.17">Ha 1:1-17</reference>. Habakkuk's Expostulation with Jehovah on Account of the Prevalence of Injustice: Jehovah Summons Attention to His Purpose of Sending the Chaldeans as the Avengers. The Prophet Complains, that These Are Worse than Those on Whom Vengeance Was to Be Taken.</title> <div sID="gen23991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12866"/><hi type="bold">1. burden--</hi>the prophetic sentence. <div eID="gen23991" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: INTRODUCTION Habakkuk, from a Hebrew root meaning to "embrace," denoting a "favorite" (namely, of God) and a "struggler" (for his country's good). Some ancient authors represent him as belonging to the tribe of Levi; others [Pseudo Epiphanius], to that of Simeon. The inscription to Bel and the dragon in the Septuagint asserts the former; and Ha 3:19 perhaps favors this. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 7.29] states that in his time Habakkuk's tomb was shown at Celia in Palestine. The time seems to have been about 610 B.C. For the Chaldeans attacked Jerusalem in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim, 605 B.C. ( 2Ki 24:1 ; 2Ch 36:6 ; Jr 46:2 ; 36:9 ). And Habakkuk ( Ha 1:5 , 6 , &c.) speaks of the Chaldeans as about to invade Judah, but not as having actually done so. In the second chapter he proceeds to comfort his people by foretelling the humiliation of their conquerors, and that the vision will soon have its fulfilment. In the third chapter the prophet in a sublime ode celebrates the deliverances wrought by Jehovah for His people in times past, as the ground of assurance, notwithstanding all their existing calamities, that He will deliver them again. Ha 3:16 shows that the invader is still coming, and not yet arrived; so that the whole refers to the invasion in Jehoiakim's times, not those under Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. The Apocryphal appendix to Daniel states that he lived to see the Babylonian exile (588 B.C.), which accords with his prophesying early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 610 B.C. The position of the book immediately after Nahum is appropriate; as Nahum treated of the judgments of the Lord on Assyria, for its violence against Israel, so Habakkuk, those inflicted by, and on, the Chaldeans for the same reason. The style is poetical and sublime. The parallelisms are generally regular. Borrowed ideas occur (compare Ha 3:19 , with Psa 18:33 ; Ha 2:6 , with Is 14:4 ; Ha 2:14 , with Is 11:9 ). The ancient catalogues imply that his book is part of the canon of Scripture. In the New Testament, Ro 1:17 quotes Ha 2:4 (though not naming him); compare also Ga 3:11 ; He 10:38 . Ac 13:40 , 41 quotes Ha 1:5 . One or two Hebrew words peculiar to Habakkuk occur ( Ha 1:9 ; 2:6, 16 ). CHAPTER 1 Ha 1:1-17 . Habakkuk's Expostulation with Jehovah on Account of the Prevalence of Injustice: Jehovah Summons Attention to His Purpose of Sending the Chaldeans as the Avengers. The Prophet Complains, that These Are Worse than Those on Whom Vengeance Was to Be Taken. 1. burden-- the prophetic sentence.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12867"/><div sID="gen23992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12867"/><hi type="bold">2-3. violence ... Why dost thou show me iniquity?--</hi>Similar language is used of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.9">Ha 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>), as here is used of the Jews: implying, that as the Jews sinned by violence and injustice, so they should be punished by violence and injustice (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>). Jehoiakim's reign was marked by injustice, treachery, and bloodshed (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">13-17</reference>). Therefore the Chaldeans should be sent to deal with him and his nobles according to their dealings with others (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">10, 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.17">17</reference>). Compare Jeremiah's expostulation with Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.8">20:8</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen23992" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2-3. violence ... Why dost thou show me iniquity?-- Similar language is used of the Chaldeans ( Ha 1:9 , 13 ), as here is used of the Jews: implying, that as the Jews sinned by violence and injustice, so they should be punished by violence and injustice ( Pr 1:31 ). Jehoiakim's reign was marked by injustice, treachery, and bloodshed ( Jr 22:3 , 13-17 ). Therefore the Chaldeans should be sent to deal with him and his nobles according to their dealings with others ( Ha 1:6 , 10, 11 , 17 ). Compare Jeremiah's expostulation with Jehovah, Jr 12:1 ; 20:8 ; and Job 19:7 , 8 .

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12870"/><div sID="gen23999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12870"/><hi type="bold">5. Behold ... marvellously ... a work--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Is 29:14</reference>). Quoted by Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>).<div eID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the heathen--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>, "ye despisers," from the Septuagint. So the Syriac and Arabic versions; perhaps from a different Hebrew reading. In the English Version reading of Habakkuk, God, in reply to the prophet's expostulation, addresses the Jews as about to be punished, "Behold ye among the heathen (with whom ye deserve to be classed, and by whom ye shall be punished, as despisers; the sense implied, which Paul expresses): learn from them what ye refused to learn from Me!" For "wonder marvellously," Paul, in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>, has, "wonder and perish," which gives the sense, not the literal wording, of the Hebrew, "Wonder, wonder," that is, be overwhelmed in wonder. The despisers are to be given up to their own stupefaction, and so perish. The Israelite unbelievers would not credit the prophecy as to the fearfulness of the destruction to be wrought by the Chaldeans, nor afterwards the deliverance promised from that nation. So analogously, in Paul's day, the Jews would not credit the judgment coming on them by the Romans, nor the salvation proclaimed through Jesus. Thus the same Scripture applied to both.<div eID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye will not believe, though it be told you--</hi>that is, ye will not believe now that I foretell it. <div eID="gen24001" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.title: Habakkuk · Original Book Introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain: INTRODUCTION Habakkuk, from a Hebrew root meaning to "embrace," denoting a "favorite" (namely, of God) and a "struggler" (for his country's good). Some ancient authors represent him as belonging to the tribe of Levi; others [Pseudo Epiphanius], to that of Simeon. The inscription to Bel and the dragon in the Septuagint asserts the former; and Ha 3:19 perhaps favors this. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 7.29] states that in his time Habakkuk's tomb was shown at Celia in Palestine. The time seems to have been about 610 B.C. For the Chaldeans attacked Jerusalem in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim, 605 B.C. ( 2Ki 24:1 ; 2Ch 36:6 ; Jr 46:2 ; 36:9 ). And Habakkuk ( Ha 1:5 , 6 , &c.) speaks of the Chaldeans as about to invade Judah, but not as having actually done so. In the second chapter he proceeds to comfort his people by foretelling the humiliation of their conquerors, and that the vision will soon have its fulfilment. In the third chapter the prophet in a sublime ode celebrates the deliverances wrought by Jehovah for His people in times past, as the ground of assurance, notwithstanding all their existing calamities, that He will deliver them again. Ha 3:16 shows that the invader is still coming, and not yet arrived; so that the whole refers to the invasion in Jehoiakim's times, not those under Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. The Apocryphal appendix to Daniel states that he lived to see the Babylonian exile (588 B.C.), which accords with his prophesying early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 610 B.C. The position of the book immediately after Nahum is appropriate; as Nahum treated of the judgments of the Lord on Assyria, for its violence against Israel, so Habakkuk, those inflicted by, and on, the Chaldeans for the same reason. The style is poetical and sublime. The parallelisms are generally regular. Borrowed ideas occur (compare Ha 3:19 , with Psa 18:33 ; Ha 2:6 , with Is 14:4 ; Ha 2:14 , with Is 11:9 ). The ancient catalogues imply that his book is part of the canon of Scripture. In the New Testament, Ro 1:17 quotes Ha 2:4 (though not naming him); compare also Ga 3:11 ; He 10:38 . Ac 13:40 , 41 quotes Ha 1:5 . One or two Hebrew words peculiar to Habakkuk occur ( Ha 1:9 ; 2:6, 16 ).
